5. Hundred Year Flood Plain
The location of a majority of the project area within the unprotected 100 year flood plain produces implications that run across the entire spectrum of environmental considerations.
Many of the actions to be taken in the project are specifically designed to deal with the "effects" of flooding; none are designed to prevent flooding. "Some are designed to lessen the negative effects of flooding."
The question arises as to the overall impact of committing State and Federal funds (translated into valuable natural resources, in terms of materials and human labor), to an unprotected 100 year flood plain area, to finance items other than flood protection measures. These items that are not essential to flood protection and that would be most obviously adversely impacted by future flooding of the project area include: (1) resources committed in the rehabilitation of properties that will remain in the area, (2) new construction resulting from redevelopment, and (3) street work and public improvements.
a. Resources Committed in the Rehabilitation of Project Properties
Urban renewal funds for rehabilitation are limited to administrative cost items and section 115 grants applicable to hardship cases. The Small Business Administration is the major source of rehabilitation funds for private property rehabilitation. Although HUD is not the major funding source for rehabilitation within the 100 year flood plain, the environmental impact of such rehabilitation must be considered as part of the project because the project includes a rehabilitation assistance program and because the project does not include provisions for the clearance of all structures within the 100 year flood plain.
